candidates.title: Map resume facts into application fields

demandEvidence.chore: Repeatedly enter resume details into company-specific application forms.
demandEvidence.evidenceQuote: I spent two hours every day filling my resume data to freshly developed forms made specifically to the hiring process of one or two companies.

candidates.whoPays: Hypothesis: job seekers who repeatedly complete company-specific application forms might pay for help; this discussion does not establish willingness to pay.

experimentPlan.output: A reviewed draft mapping of supplied resume facts to a small set of manually copied application fields.
inputs: A fictional resume with verified work and education facts
A manually supplied sample form field list
A mapping table of each field to its resume source
An operator supplied rule for fields that must remain unanswered
experimentPlan.trigger: A job seeker supplies one target form field list and asks for a draft mapping.
steps: Extract only facts explicitly present in the supplied resume.
Match each requested field to a resume fact or mark it unknown.
Draft concise field values without adding qualifications or dates.
Show each value with its source fact for review.
Have the person correct the mapping and enter or submit every answer manually.
experimentPlan.acceptanceCheck: On fictional resume and form pairs, every drafted value must match a cited resume fact, unknown fields must remain blank, and a person must approve all entries.
experimentPlan.humanBoundary: The job seeker supplies the resume and field list, verifies each value, handles sensitive application data, and enters and submits the form; no live form access is proposed.
unverified: Whether common application fields repeat enough across forms to be useful
Reliable extraction from varied resume formats
Any live browser or application integration
Whether job seekers would pay for the proposed assistance

ease.reason: A manually supplied resume and field list allow a small mock, but no implementation reference is available.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: job seekers may value less repetitive entry, but the post establishes no buyer intent or payment.

feasibility.reason: A four-week mock can map a few supplied fields; varied forms and extraction quality remain untested.

autonomy.reason: The proposed mapping can repeat, but a person must verify and submit every field; no automation capability is documented.

evidence.reason: The post directly reports daily resume entry for forms tailored to one or two companies, without field examples or corroboration.

candidates.reason: Below threshold: the literal chore supports a narrow manual-input mapping experiment, but there is no implementation reference, broader demand evidence, or supported live-form capability.

candidates.title: Draft daily summaries from order records

demandEvidence.chore: Generate daily summaries of completed orders, cancellations, and pending requests.
demandEvidence.evidenceQuote: Daily reports: Generate summaries of completed orders, cancellations, and pending requests.

candidates.whoPays: Hypothesis: operators of multi-service platforms might pay for report preparation; the discussion establishes no buyer intent or payment.

experimentPlan.output: A concise daily summary counting completed, canceled, and pending orders from supplied sample rows.
inputs: Fictional order rows with an order identifier
A supplied order status for each row
A proposed summary format with counts and exceptions
experimentPlan.trigger: An operator starts a daily test run after supplying that day’s sample order rows.
steps: Check that each supplied row has an identifier and one of the supplied statuses.
Group rows into completed, canceled, and pending categories.
Calculate category counts from the supplied rows.
Draft a short summary and list rows with missing or unrecognized statuses.
Compare every count against the source rows and have an operator approve the report.
experimentPlan.acceptanceCheck: For a fixed fictional dataset, each category count must equal a manual count of matching rows, and every missing or unrecognized status must be listed instead of silently classified.
experimentPlan.humanBoundary: An operator defines the statuses and reporting format, supplies records, checks counts and exceptions, and approves any report; no access to a real platform or production data is proposed.
unverified: Whether operators have this recurring reporting need
The production platform data fields and access method
Whether the proposed draft can be generated reliably
Whether any supplied integration can schedule or persist reports

ease.reason: A beginner can test counting and summarizing fictional rows, but no supplied implementation reference supports automation.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: multi-service platform operators might pay for reporting help; the idea post gives no buyer or payment evidence.

feasibility.reason: A four-week sample-data prototype is bounded, though production fields and accuracy remain unknown.

autonomy.reason: A proposed batch can draft a report, but no execution capability is documented and a person must validate it.

evidence.reason: The post names daily reports and three order states, but gives no field details, examples, or corroboration.

candidates.reason: Below threshold: a sample-data report draft is assessable, but implementation support and evidence of a recurring unmet need are limited.

rejected.title: How to report IP abuse to Cloudflare?
rejected.reason: The retained demand text is only “which clearly doesn’t apply here.” These spans do not identify a concrete reporting task or enough context to infer one, so no chore or experiment is invented.

rejected.title: Dinemic – self-hosted ingress across providers
rejected.reason: This is a maker description of a tool’s design goal around hosting-provider redundancy, not an external request or concrete unmet customer chore. The supplied excerpt supports no demand-first experiment.

rejected.title: Enable Execute Command in self-hosted n8n
rejected.reason: The original-post spans describe a one-off configuration troubleshooting question about an unavailable node. This is a product support issue, not a repeatable service demand suitable for an AI business experiment.

rejected.title: WhatsApp agents and booking automations
rejected.reason: The retained spans are a provider’s service list and self-promotion, including existing examples, rather than a request for help. They do not establish an unmet chore or buyer need.

rejected.title: Weekly keyword volume to Google Sheets
rejected.reason: The retained text describes an already built weekly workflow and its operating schedule and cost. It is a maker demonstration, not evidence of an unmet customer chore.

rejected.title: Make.com automation for simple business tasks
rejected.reason: The post is an offer to perform small automation jobs and lists broad capabilities, but supplies no specific requested task from a customer. The offer itself does not establish demand for a distinct experiment.

steps.message: Assessed all eight sealed discussion assignments. Two concrete chores received scoped experiment plans and five provisional ratings; both remain below threshold. The other six lack a concrete unmet chore or are support/maker posts. No post proposed.
